passages.t: An everlasting love, and dancing again
passages.happening:
The LORD says that at that time he will be the God of all the families of Israel, and they will be his people (verse 1). The people who survived the sword found favor in the wilderness (verse 2). ‘I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have drawn you with loving devotion’ (verse 3).

‘Again I will build you, and you will be rebuilt, O Virgin Israel’ (verse 4). Again they will take up tambourines and dance, plant vineyards on the hills of Samaria and enjoy the fruit (verses 4 and 5). Watchmen on the hills of Ephraim will call people up to Zion (verse 6).

God will bring them from the land of the north and from the ends of the earth, the blind and the lame, mothers and women in labor, a great company (verse 8). ‘They will come with weeping, and by their supplication I will lead them’ (verse 9), by streams on a level path. ‘For I am Israel’s Father, and Ephraim is My firstborn’ (verse 9). The One who scattered Israel will gather and keep him as a shepherd keeps his flock (verse 10). ‘I will turn their mourning into joy, and give them comfort and joy for their sorrow’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The chapter carries no date, and its parts may come from different moments. The poems to Ephraim and Samaria fit Jeremiah's early years under Josiah, from about 640 to 609 BC, when Assyria was collapsing and Josiah pushed north into the old land of Israel. A prophet then could speak of Ephraim coming home as a real prospect. Some scholars think an early form was spoken to the north and later reworked for Judah after 587 BC.

Ephraim was the leading tribe of the northern kingdom, often standing for the whole north. Its people had been taken by Assyria a century before. God calls Ephraim his firstborn, the son with the double portion.

The company coming home includes the blind, the lame and women about to give birth, the people who would usually be left behind on a long march. No one is left out of this return.
passages.later: A psalm sings the same reversal: ‘You turned my mourning into dancing’ (Psalm 30:11). Hosea hears God's heart for Ephraim in the same way: ‘How could I give you up, O Ephraim?’ (Hosea 11:8).
passages.asks: God says he has loved his people with an everlasting love. Ask what it would mean to believe that about yourself. And ask whom God might be bringing home that others would leave behind on the road.

passages.t: Rachel weeping, and Ephraim a precious son
passages.happening:
‘A voice is heard in Ramah, mourning and great weeping, Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more’ (verse 15).

God answers her. ‘Keep your voice from weeping and your eyes from tears, for the reward for your work will come’ (verse 16), and her children will come back from the land of the enemy. ‘So there is hope for your future, declares the LORD, and your children will return to their own land’ (verse 17).

God has heard Ephraim's moaning: Ephraim says he was disciplined like an untrained calf and asks God to bring him back (verse 18). After he turned, he repented and struck his thigh in grief (verse 19). ‘Is not Ephraim a precious son to Me, a delightful child?’ (verse 20). Though God often speaks against him, he still remembers him, and his heart yearns for him (verse 20).

The daughter of Israel is told to set up road markers and come back by the way she went (verse 21). God has created a new thing on earth (verse 22). People will again speak well of Jerusalem's holy mountain (verse 23). ‘For I will refresh the weary soul and replenish all who are weak’ (verse 25). Then the prophet wakes, and his sleep had been sweet (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Rachel was Jacob's beloved wife, the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, and so the ancestress of Ephraim and the northern tribes. Ramah, a town north of Jerusalem in Benjamin, was where the Babylonians later gathered the captives before marching them away, and Jeremiah himself was released there in chapter 40. Jeremiah pictures Rachel, long dead, weeping over her descendants as they are led into exile. God tells her to stop weeping. They will come back.

Striking the thigh was a gesture of grief and shame. Ephraim's turning back is told in his own words.

The new thing of verse 22, a woman encompassing a man, is one of the hardest lines in the book to translate, and readers have proposed many meanings. It seems to mean some reversal as surprising as the return itself.

Verse 26 suggests this comfort came to Jeremiah in a dream or vision. For once, the prophet of doom woke from a sweet sleep.
passages.later: Matthew sets verse 15 beside the grief of Bethlehem's mothers when Herod killed their children: “Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more” (Matthew 2:18).
passages.hard:
Matthew says Herod's killing of the children at Bethlehem fulfilled Rachel's weeping. Isn't he taking a verse about the exile out of its setting?

The objection has two parts. Verse 15 plainly describes the exile of Rachel's descendants in the sixth century BC, and it is not phrased as a prediction. And the massacre is recorded nowhere outside Matthew; some scholars, Raymond Brown among them, have judged the story more likely a theological narrative patterned on Pharaoh's killing of Hebrew boys than a historical report.

The answers begin with what Matthew means by fulfill. Most commentators, including those who defend the story's history, agree that Matthew is not claiming Jeremiah foresaw Bethlehem. He reads Israel's history as a pattern that comes to its fullness in Jesus, as he does with Hosea 11:1 in the same chapter. His choice is careful: Ramah was where the exiles were gathered, Rachel's tomb was remembered near Bethlehem, and Jeremiah's lament is followed at once by the promise that the children will come home.

If you carry grief or guilt about a pregnancy, or about the loss of a child before or after birth, please know that you are met with gentleness here, not judgment. God knows your story too. Please talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Rachel would not be comforted, and God spoke to her grief. Ask whose grief you are tempted to hurry past. And ask what it means for you that God still remembers Ephraim, even after speaking against him so often.

passages.t: A new covenant written on the heart
passages.happening:
The days are coming when God will sow Israel and Judah with people and animals (verse 27). As he watched over them to uproot and tear down, so he will watch over them ‘to build and to plant’ (verse 28). No one will say any more that the fathers ate sour grapes and the children's teeth are set on edge (verse 29). ‘Instead, each will die for his own iniquity’ (verse 30).

‘Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah’ (verse 31). It will not be like the covenant made when God took their fathers by the hand to lead them out of Egypt, the covenant they broke, though he was a husband to them (verse 32). ‘I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people’ (verse 33). No one will need to teach his neighbor to know the LORD, ‘because they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest’ (verse 34). ‘For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more’ (verse 34).

The God who gives the sun by day and the moon and stars by night says that only if that fixed order left his presence would Israel's descendants cease to be a nation before him (verses 35 and 36). Only if the heavens could be measured would he reject them (verse 37). The city will be rebuilt for the LORD, and even the valley of the dead and of ashes will be holy to him (verses 38 to 40).
passages.hearers:
The proverb of sour grapes said the children were paying for their fathers' sins. The exiles felt it. God answers that in the coming days each will answer for his own. Ezekiel takes up the same proverb.

The covenant at Sinai was written on tablets of stone. Its weakness was not in the law itself but in hearts that would not keep it. The new covenant is still God's law, now written on the heart, so that knowing God is no longer something taught from outside but known from within. And it rests on forgiveness: God will remember their sins no more.

The promise is made to the house of Israel and the house of Judah. Verses 35 to 37 bind God to Israel's descendants as firmly as to the sun and stars.

The valley of the dead and of ashes is likely the Valley of Hinnom, the place of Topheth. Even the place of the worst sin will be made holy.
passages.later: At the Last Supper Jesus took the cup and said, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you” (Luke 22:20). Hebrews 8 quotes verses 31 to 34 in full, ‘I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah’ (Hebrews 8:8), and Hebrews 10:16-17 returns to it.
passages.hard:
The new covenant is promised to the house of Israel and the house of Judah. How can Christians claim it?

The strongest objection comes from Jewish readers, and it is textual. The promise is addressed to Israel and Judah, not to the nations; it speaks of God's law written on hearts, not set aside; and it describes a world in which everyone in the covenant knows the LORD. Medieval Jewish commentators such as David Kimhi read it as the covenant of Sinai at last kept faithfully, and modern historical critics add that Jeremiah meant a national renewal after the exile.

Christians agree that Jesus began the new covenant through his death, since he said so at the Last Supper and Hebrews quotes this passage to explain it, and that believers from every nation share its forgiveness and its Spirit. They explain the rest in different ways. Many in the Reformed tradition hold that the church, Jewish and Gentile believers together in Christ, is the renewed Israel to whom the promise belongs, with its full scope awaiting Christ's return. Dispensational interpreters distinguish the church's present share in its spiritual gifts from national promises to Israel still to come. Others see Christ as the true Israel in whom the promise is kept for all who belong to him. On the charge that the promise has not come, most Christians answer that it has begun but is not complete.

This is a second-order question on which faithful Christians disagree. All should grant that verses 35 to 37 bind God to Israel's descendants as firmly as to the sun and stars, and all should reject contempt for the Jewish people, whom Paul calls ‘loved on account of the patriarchs’ (Romans 11:28).
passages.asks: God promises to write his law on the heart and remember sins no more. Ask what it would mean for you to know God from within rather than only from being taught. And ask which of your sins you are still remembering that God has promised to forget.
